Inspect the public exampleUse the template

4. Hand-and-product scale

A hand supplies scale and human context, but should not hide the label.

Close beauty photograph of a natural hand holding the exact reference product at chest height. Fingers rest behind the vessel and do not cover the front label, pump or cap. Preserve packaging geometry and materials; realistic skin texture and anatomy, soft window light, neutral background, vertical 4:5.
Replace “reference” with the product, model, or scene you upload.
Inspect the public exampleUse the template

5. Bathroom routine

Give the product a credible use context without visual clutter.

The exact reference beauty product beside a folded white towel and clear water glass on a pale stone bathroom shelf. Preserve the package exactly and keep the front label unobstructed. Early morning window light, fine condensation in the background only, calm editorial composition, vertical 4:5.
Replace “reference” with the product, model, or scene you upload.
Use the template

6. Ingredient overhead

Build a visual ingredient story without making unsupported claims.

Overhead still life of the exact reference beauty product centered among a small number of supplied ingredient references. Preserve packaging geometry and label placement. Arrange ingredients with deliberate spacing on warm ivory paper, soft directional daylight, realistic shadows, no medical symbols, no added text, 4:5.
Replace “reference” with the product, model, or scene you upload.
Use the template

7. Collection trio

Prove relative scale and keep a product family coherent.

Studio group photograph of the three exact reference beauty products arranged from tallest to shortest on stepped ivory plinths. Preserve each vessel, closure, label position, color and relative size. Soft frontal light with a narrow rim highlight, no overlap across labels, clean pale background, vertical 4:5.
Replace “reference” with the product, model, or scene you upload.
Use the template

8. Wide campaign banner

Leave deliberate copy space for a landing page or paid-social crop.

Wide beauty campaign still life with the exact reference product in the right third on a low mineral plinth. Preserve the packaging exactly. Soft lilac-to-ivory gradient, long controlled shadow, generous clean negative space on the left, no generated text, crisp premium light, horizontal 16:9.
Replace “reference” with the product, model, or scene you upload.
Use the template

What changes by challenge​

ChallengePrompt forCheck before approval
Reflective glassOne controlled softbox reflectionNo doubled edges or clipped highlights
Pumps and droppersExact closure geometry and orientationStem, collar and cap remain physically plausible
Transparent formulaColor, opacity and viscosityFormula does not become milk, gel or water accidentally
LabelsPosition and layout, not invented wordingCompare every visible character with approved artwork
Hands and skinNatural anatomy and unobstructed packageFive fingers, believable grip, readable product

How to use these prompts​

  1. Photograph or upload the front, side, closure and important material details.
  2. Generate the clean packshot and approve geometry first.
  3. Copy one prompt, replace generic nouns with facts from the references, and change one scene variable at a time.
  4. Compare results as a set at full size and thumbnail size.
  5. Composite approved label artwork when exact legal or retail copy must be guaranteed.

For the wider e-commerce system, including coverage planning and evaluation, continue with E-commerce Product Photography Prompts.

Frequently asked questions​

What should a beauty product prompt include?​

Specify the product construction, view, surface, light behavior, composition and format separately.

How do I keep cosmetic packaging accurate?​

Use several clean reference views, prove the product in a plain packshot, then verify the final result against approved packaging artwork.

Which beauty images belong on a product page?​

Start with a front, alternate angle, closure or applicator, formula texture, scale cue, routine context and one campaign frame.

item.title: Ghost Mannequin Alternatives: Which Workflow to Choose (2026)
item.description: Compare flat lay, hanger, live-model and AI on-model alternatives to ghost mannequin photography. Decide what to replace, what to keep, and how to test the switch.
item.content:encoded:
The best ghost mannequin alternative depends on what you want to stop doing. Dressing forms, waiting for neck composites, and showing clothes without a person are three different problems. They do not need the same replacement.

The short version: use flat lay when you need a simpler product-only view, a live model when the worn garment needs to be documented, and AI on-model when you have approved product references and need more styling options. Keep ghost mannequin where its clean, body-shaped presentation still earns its place.

Upfront disclosure: Astria publishes this guide and offers AI fashion imagery. The comparisons below are editorial production judgments, not results from a timed vendor benchmark.

Reviewed September 5, 2026. Service descriptions were checked against first-party sources. No universal cost saving or conversion lift is assumed.

Fashion production workspace

Create your next campaign with Astria

Generate fashion visuals from your products, or start with a production-ready template.

Generate→Templates gallery→

An Astria example: dress photo to packshot

Compare the original dress with the generated image, especially the neckline, seams, and hem.

This shows an Astria result. The other service was not tested with this same photo.

View this generationTry the dress template

Choose the alternative by the work it removes​

RouteWhat changes in productionWhat the image gives youWhat you still have to solve
Keep ghost mannequinDress a form, capture hidden areas, join the viewsIsolated garment with body volumeStyling, accurate joins, and product review
Outsource the compositeMove masking and joining to a retouching serviceThe same ghost mannequin formatPhysical capture and approval remain with your team
Flat layArrange and photograph the garment on a surfaceUnobstructed product shape, graphics, and details in a flat stateBody volume and worn appearance need other views
Hanger photographSuspend the garment and photograph itA hanging silhouette with no personThe hanger affects shoulders and supplies no torso volume
Live-model photographSchedule a wearer, style the sample, shoot selected posesObserved drape and proportions on that personSample fit, shoot coordination, and retouching
AI on-modelPrepare references, choose a treatment, generate, review, correctA generated worn presentation and styling optionsProduct fidelity, invented drape, and rejected outputs

These are workflow differences, not speed rankings. A heavily styled flat lay can consume more time than a familiar mannequin setup. An AI image that needs repeated correction can miss a deadline that a short model session would meet.

If you already know you want to keep the hollow garment format, use the ghost mannequin capture and compositing guide. If you have chosen AI on-model and need source preparation, use flat lay to on-model.

When the bottleneck is editing, keep the format​

A queue of unfinished collars is a capacity problem. Changing the entire catalog to on-model imagery introduces casting, styling, and gallery decisions before it fixes that queue.

Pixelz describes its ghost mannequin service as combining multiple supplied product images in post-production, with manual, FTP, and API upload options. That is a concrete alternative to making every composite in-house. It still needs the source photographs.

Before switching formats, ask a retouching provider to process a representative set using your existing crop, garment shape, and color standard. Compare revision time and accepted results with the current process. If the catalog presentation is already useful, moving the joining work may be enough.

An AI tool that produces another hollow garment image is also preserving the format. Ask which visible areas come from supplied photographs and which are generated. A plausible invented lining is a different deliverable from a composite of the photographed lining.

When you need simpler product-only capture​

Flat lay is the clearest alternative when chest or hip volume is not the point of the image. A graphic tee may need its print shown without folds crossing the design. A matching set may need both pieces visible together. There is no reason to create an invisible torso for every such view.

Shopify's clothing photography guide describes flat lay as an overhead view on a surface and distinguishes it from model, mannequin, and lifestyle photography. It also recommends planning the angles and detail views needed for each product. A simpler setup does not eliminate the shot list.

A hanger is another option when the suspended garment reads well and fits the brand's presentation. Judge the actual sample: if the shoulders collapse, the neckline stretches, or the body hangs like a narrow tube, the hanger has removed information you needed. Keeping the hanger visible can be more straightforward than retouching it out and reconstructing the area behind it.

Our recommendation: choose these formats for their useful product view, then account for any missing view elsewhere in the gallery. Do not treat a single flat lay as an equivalent replacement for a front, back, and volume set.

When a person is the missing information​

Live-model photography is the strongest choice when the buying question concerns the actual garment on a body: where a sleeve ends, how a skirt falls when standing, or what an open jacket reveals.

The photograph records one sample, one wearer, one pose, and any styling adjustments. It does not prove how every size fits every shopper. Record the model's measurements and sample size, and avoid pinning that changes the feature you are trying to show.

For a dress whose appeal is its drape, a short, controlled shoot may be a more useful investment than perfecting a hollow silhouette. Keep separate detail views for features that hair, hands, or styling obscure.

This is a decision about what to document. A brand can still use ghost mannequin for the clean front view and a real wearer for the side profile or movement. There is no requirement to make every gallery slot use the same format.

When AI on-model is a useful replacement​

AI on-model is worth testing when the missing asset is a styled presentation and the product has already been photographed clearly. It can make an existing reference library useful in more contexts. It also introduces a new approval task: checking that the rendered garment still describes the item being sold.

Pixelz's August 2026 synthetic-model workflow starts with real product imagery, prepares it before generation, reviews the generated result, and sends selected outputs through final post-production. Its description supports the practical boundary: generation is one stage of production, and convincing outputs can still contain product errors. This is a vendor-described process, not evidence of an approval rate.

Astria's ecommerce workflow lets brands select creative templates, upload product photographs, and generate imagery for lookbooks, social, and campaigns. For a team moving beyond product-only presentation, that provides a route to test an on-model treatment using existing inputs.

Our recommendation is to start with a garment whose identity you can verify from the references. Approve the neckline, sleeve length, print placement, seams, closures, and opacity before judging whether you like the model or background. If the generated image supplies a back view that you never photographed, it has not established what the back looks like.

Keep a physical worn view when drape or fit is the selling point and the generated result cannot be checked adequately. AI on-model is a visual interpretation, not a measurement-based fit test. The virtual try-on guide covers that distinction in more detail.

Decide what leaves the gallery, not just what enters it​

A practical replacement brief names a gallery slot and the information it must retain. “Replace ghost mannequin” is too broad.

Example briefSensible decisionCondition for making the switch
Basic tee needs a clearer graphic viewTest flat lay as the product-only frontFull graphic and garment proportions remain readable
Tailored blazer needs its structured shape shown without a personKeep ghost mannequin; improve or outsource the compositeThe existing format serves the requirement
Dress needs evidence of worn length and fallAdd or prioritize a live-model viewSample size, wearer, and styling are documented
Existing ghost images are accurate, but the gallery needs outfit contextAdd an approved AI on-model imageStyling does not hide or alter product-defining features
New drop has no usable product photographsCapture references before selecting an AI routeThe actual colorway and construction can be verified

These examples are recommendations for a pilot, not claims that a garment category always succeeds in one format.

An old ghost mannequin image does not become obsolete when an AI model arrives. If it still gives shoppers a clearer view of the product, keep it. The alternative may replace the next shoot's presentation work while leaving useful existing assets in service.

Compare the cost of a complete approved gallery​

A price per composite and a price per generation buy different things. For this decision, use the cost per SKU with its required gallery approved.

Count sample preparation, capture, outside fees, generation, retouching, operator time, reviewer time, and corrections. Include a physical shoot fallback for products the alternative cannot handle. For planning, allocate shared setup across the expected batch and value internal time at the same rate in each route.

Then count coverage. A cheaper front image is not a saving if it requires a new side image to recover information the original showed. Conversely, keeping an approved ghost image and adding one useful on-model view may cost less than replacing the entire set.

For a numeric costing framework, use product photography cost per SKU. For the broader allocation of studio and AI work across campaigns, see AI product photography versus a packshot studio.

Run a six-SKU replacement test​

Choose two routine items, two recurring production problems, and two difficult products from your own range. This is a suggested operational sample, not a statistically representative experiment.

  1. Name the bottleneck. Record whether you want to reduce dressing time, composite revisions, shoot scheduling, or missing on-model coverage.
  2. Fix the gallery brief. Require the same product information, output dimensions, and deadline for the current route and the candidate alternative. Preserve the approved physical references.
  3. Set acceptance rules before production. Product-changing errors are failures. Name who checks them, and set a revision limit after which the SKU returns to physical capture or the existing workflow.
  4. Record the whole job. Track elapsed time, human minutes, outside spend, rejected outputs, missing views, and whether each complete gallery passes. Count failed attempts and fallback work.
  5. Switch only the passing group. If basics pass and patterned items do not, use separate routes. Keep the current gallery available until the replacement is approved.

Check the destination channel's current image requirements before making a candidate your main image. For Amazon, start with the apparel image guide and the category-specific source it points to.

Production approval and sales performance are separate questions. After the accuracy review, test gallery presentation with your own traffic. Do not attribute a sales change to on-model imagery if the same launch also changed pricing, promotions, or assortment.

Frequently asked questions​

What is the best alternative to ghost mannequin photography?​

Choose flat lay for a simple product-only view, hanger photography for a suspended presentation, live-model photography to document the garment worn by a real person, or AI on-model imagery for styling variations from approved references. Keep ghost mannequin when isolated body volume is the requirement. The best choice depends on the job of the image.

Can AI replace a ghost mannequin shoot?​

AI can replace some new presentation work when suitable product references already exist and the outputs pass review. It does not remove the need to document the garment. If a generated image changes seams, print placement, opacity, or proportions, use a corrected output or physical photography instead.

Is outsourcing ghost mannequin retouching an alternative?​

It is an alternative to doing the composite in-house, but it keeps the ghost mannequin format and source-photography requirements. Consider it when editing capacity is the bottleneck and the existing product presentation already works.

Is flat lay cheaper than ghost mannequin photography?​

Flat lay can avoid mannequin dressing and interior compositing, but styling, capture, retouching, and approval still take time. Compare the total cost of an approved product gallery with the same required views, including any extra images needed to explain volume or worn appearance.

Should I remove existing ghost mannequin images when adding AI models?​

Keep accurate existing images while testing the new format. A product-only view and an approved on-model image can serve different gallery roles. Remove a ghost mannequin view only when its replacement covers the same information and the remaining gallery still represents the product accurately.

Sources and methodology​

Research checked September 5, 2026: Shopify's clothing photography guide, Pixelz's ghost mannequin service, Pixelz's synthetic-model production account, and Astria's ecommerce product page. These are first-party descriptions of formats and services. The decision tables and pilot are our editorial recommendations; no side-by-side production trial was conducted for this article. The cover is an AI-generated editorial illustration, not a tested product conversion.

2. GoPackshot: managed physical production​

GoPackshot is the closest match for a buyer who means, “Take our products and return ecommerce-ready assets.” Its services page describes packshot, model, ghost-mannequin and flat-lay photography; video and 360-degree content; product logistics; retouching; quality control; and delivery into brand systems.

The important word is managed. You ship physical inventory and buy an operating service, not a self-serve 3D application. That makes GoPackshot a credible choice when color, garment construction, marketplace rules, product handling, and accountability matter more than owning the capture line.

GoPackshot also publishes claims about color tolerances, daily capacity, studio count, integrations, and tracked logistics. Treat those as vendor-reported claims, then put the relevant ones into the contract or test brief. A public capacity number does not establish capacity for your garment mix, revision policy, or launch window.

Its public service description includes 360-degree video, but does not describe the output as a freely navigable GLB or USDZ model. If you need true 3D, ask three blunt questions:

  1. Is the deliverable an image sequence, video, web viewer, or model file?
  2. Can the shopper move to an angle that was never photographed?
  3. Do we receive geometry, materials, dimensions, and usage rights?

If the answers are “sequence,” “no,” and “no,” you are buying a photographic spin. That can be an excellent asset. It is not a true 3D model.

3. Orbitvu: bring automated capture in-house​

Orbitvu sells automated photography systems rather than operating as your outsourced packshot studio. Its ecommerce product line covers stills, 360-degree images and video; its fashion positioning includes ghost mannequin, flat lay, on-figure work, and standardized footwear angles.

This route changes the economics. Instead of paying a service per project or SKU, you own equipment, studio utilization, operators, styling, color management, maintenance, and workflow integration. The best candidate already has products moving through one facility and a team that can keep a capture recipe stable.

Vendor language such as “web-ready content in minutes” is vendor-reported and should be separated into capture time, operator touch time, retouching time, rework, and publishing time. A fast turntable does not dress a mannequin, correct a crushed collar, approve color, or resolve a barcode mismatch.

Choose Orbitvu when the problem is repeatable physical capture at sustained volume. Do not choose it because the word “360” appears near “3D.” Confirm the exact output your selected system produces.

4. PhotoRobot: automated capture with a wider output menu​

PhotoRobot also sells hardware and workflow software for in-house or studio operators. Its public output gallery explicitly separates still images, 360 spins, “3D spins,” photogrammetry 3D models, and 360 video. That taxonomy is useful because it exposes how different outputs are often grouped under one marketing label.

For fashion, PhotoRobot sells ghost-mannequin equipment and describes workflows for stills, spins, and ecommerce 3D models. Those are vendor-reported capabilities. Ask to see an output from the same product class and material as yours: a matte sneaker is not evidence for patent leather; a rigid bag is not evidence for a soft dress.

PhotoRobot is the more relevant shortlist entry when you want a configurable automated studio and may need several capture modes. The procurement risk is complexity: a system that can produce five asset types still needs five acceptance standards.

5. Threekit: true 3D, configuration, and AR​

Threekit belongs in the shortlist only when the buying problem is interactive 3D rather than photography. Its platform overview distinguishes virtual photography, WebGL-based interactive 3D, and augmented reality. Its platform can create glTF and USDZ variants for web AR and supports configurable products whose visual state changes with selected options.

That is a materially different deliverable. The shopper can interact with geometry and materials, and the same product definition can support many configurations. It is especially relevant to customizable bags, footwear, jewelry, furniture, equipment, or other structured products where options and spatial understanding affect purchase.

The hard part is the asset system behind the viewer. Before buying, scope who creates the base geometry, materials, variant logic, dimensions, and future revisions. Threekit publishes commercial performance statistics; treat every such number as a vendor-reported result, not a forecast for your store.

For a single non-configurable garment, this can be more system than the buying question deserves. For a configurable product family, it may be the only category here that actually solves the problem.

6. VNTANA: optimize and distribute models you already have​

VNTANA is best understood as a 3D asset pipeline. Its 3D commerce page describes taking existing CAD or 3D files, optimizing them, and distributing web-ready 3D and AR assets to commerce channels.

That is valuable when product development already produces usable 3D assets. It is not the same as shipping a garment to a photography studio. Ask whether model creation or cleanup is included in your scope, because “upload your 3D file” assumes the most expensive input may already exist.

VNTANA publishes performance claims for 3D commerce; those are vendor-reported. Evaluate the platform on file reduction, visual fidelity after optimization, variant handling, viewer performance, publishing integrations, and the labor saved in your actual catalog.

7. Shopify Partners: bounded custom model production​

For a Shopify merchant with a small, prioritized model list, the most direct procurement path may be a 3D-modeling partner rather than an enterprise platform. Shopify’s partner guidance says a modeler may need multi-angle photographs, dimensions in millimeters, diagrams, and CAD files where available. It also provides a practical review checklist for shape, scale, materials, reflections, textures, edges, and unwanted gaps.

Shopify says the delivered model should be a GLB, approximately 4 MB and no more than 15 MB under the guidance on that page. Recheck current limits before commissioning because platform requirements change. Your theme must also support the media type; see the Shopify product media guide before approving the project.

This route is strong when true 3D is needed for ten important products, not ten thousand speculative ones.

Do not ask each supplier for “a 3D packshot quote.” Send one matrix and require every cell to be answered.

How Astria fits with physical capture and true 3D​

Astria should be scored on the asset it actually delivers: a fast AI-generated rotation video and angle stills from one fashion flat lay. It should not be scored as a true 3D modeling bureau.

The strongest hybrid uses an approved packshot or well-lit flat lay as Astria’s input, reviews the inferred views against the physical SKU, and publishes the MP4 where rotation communicates shape or drape. Keep calibrated photography for exact color and construction evidence. Buy true 3D only when arbitrary viewing, configuration, or AR is the requirement.

Frequently asked questions​

What is the best 3D packshot service for ecommerce?​

There is no single best service because several different purchases share the name. Choose Astria for a fast AI-generated fashion rotation video and angle stills from one flat lay, a managed studio for approved physical photography and captured spins, capture equipment for a repeatable in-house studio, a model-creation partner for a true GLB or USDZ, and a 3D commerce platform for configuration, AR, or multi-channel delivery.

Where does Astria fit among 3D packshot services?​

Astria is the fast AI-generated option for fashion. Its 3D ghost packshot workflow takes one flat-lay photo and returns a six-second 1080p rotation video plus three angle stills for social and product pages. It does not return an interactive GLB or USDZ model, and inferred views still require product-accuracy review.

Does GoPackshot create true interactive 3D models?​

GoPackshot's public services page describes packshot photography, ghost mannequin, video, and 360-degree content within a managed physical production service. It does not present those outputs as freely navigable GLB or USDZ models. Ask for the exact deliverable, viewer, and file format rather than assuming that 360 means true 3D.

Is a 360 spin the same as a 3D product model?​

No. A photographic 360 spin is a sequence of captured angles. A true 3D model contains geometry and materials, can usually be viewed from arbitrary angles, and may support augmented reality. Some vendors use the word “3D” for a spin effect, so inspect the exported file and interaction rather than the label.

When should a brand buy automated 360 capture equipment?​

Buy equipment when physical products already flow through one location, the shot recipe is stable, utilization will be high, and the team can own styling, color management, maintenance, and quality control. Outsource when volume is irregular or operational ownership would sit with nobody.

What should be included in a 3D packshot quote?​

A comparable quote should name the source inputs, output files, number of views or model variants, polygon and texture budgets, color and dimension tolerances, AR support, viewer or hosting fees, revision rounds, ownership, turnaround, and what happens when the physical product changes.
